meaning: 'Hard to Conquer in Battle' (dur- 'hard' + yodhana 'fighting') — the eldest Kaurava, rival of the Pāṇḍavas whose refusal to yield their share of the kingdom brings about the Kurukṣetra war

phonemes.desc: The prefix dur- means “hard, ill” — the same intensifier as in “duress”.
From yudh, “fight”: yodhana, “fighting”. The compound is transparent: hard to conquer in battle.
The dh is a voiced aspirate; the name his mother chose against his father’s better judgement.

kin.label: Birth-name
kin.form: Suyodhana — “good in battle”; the name was changed by the Pāṇḍavas’ jibe

pronunciation.note: He was born Suyodhana; the jeering name by which history knows him is itself a piece of the epic’s blame-work.

domains.title: Hard to Conquer in Battle
domains.subtitle: The Eldest Kaurava, Rival of the Pāṇḍavas
domains.lead: Duryodhana is the Mahābhārata’s tragic antagonist: the eldest of the hundred Kauravas, peerless mace-fighter, generous friend, and the man whose refusal to yield an inch of the kingdom brought the world to war. The epic refuses to make him a villain simple enough to hate — his claim is legally arguable, his grievance real, and his end the war’s most earned lamentation.

cards.name: The Hundredth Son
cards.desc: Born of Gandhārī’s split pregnancy as a ball of flesh, divided into a hundred sons by Vyāsa’s grace.

cards.name: Mace-Master
cards.desc: The equal of Bhīma with the gadā; his duel with Bhīma closes the war’s eighteenth day.

cards.name: Friend of Karṇa
cards.desc: The epic’s one unbreakable friendship: the outcast-sūta king he crowned against all caste law.

cards.name: The Dice Refusal
cards.desc: “Not a needle’s point of land” — the sentence that made the Kurukṣetra war inevitable.

mythology.lead: Duryodhana’s mythology is the Mahābhārata read from the losing side: the crown prince displaced by cousins the law favoured, the commander whose every general was better than his cause. The epic gives him the war’s best exit-line and its most human griefs — for Karṇa, for his sons, and for the pride he would not trade for peace.

myths.title: The Ball of Flesh
myths.text: Gandhārī carried her pregnancy two years; delivered of a hard mass of flesh, she was about to cast it away when Vyāsa ordered it divided — a hundred pieces in oil-jars, and one more that became Duhśalā. Duryodhana’s birth-omen — braying donkeys, circling vultures — had the elders counselling his abandonment; Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s love overruled the omen, and the epic marks the moment the world’s fate turned.

myths.title: The Dice Game
myths.text: At Śakuni’s loaded board, Duryodhana won the Pāṇḍavas’ kingdom, their liberty, and their queen — and ordered Duḥśāsana to drag Draupadī to the court. Her question — what did you stake first, the kingdom or me? — unmade his legal victory and made his moral one: he returned the stakes and later the kingdom, but the insult outlived the restitution.

myths.title: The Embassies and the Refusal
myths.text: Krishna came in peace, then as war-herald; the Pāṇḍavas asked for five villages. ‘I will not give the Pāṇḍavas land equal to the point of a needle’ — Duryodhana’s answer to Krishna’s peace-mission is the epic’s hinge. Every reader who has wished he’d yielded has made the epic’s point: the war was chosen, not fated.

myths.title: The Last Duel
myths.text: On the war’s final day Duryodhana, alone of the hundred, met Bhīma by the lake of blood. Equal until the last, he fell to the mace-blow Bhīma aimed below the belt — the one illegal stroke of their duel, urged by Krishna. The epic lets the ‘good’ side win by the foul its cause had licensed; Duryodhana’s dying reproach stands unanswered in the text.

lore.syncretism: Duryodhana is the epic’s dark mirror of the dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira: where the eldest Pāṇḍava keeps the letter and loses the spirit, Duryodhana keeps the pride and loses everything. Later tradition made him a byword for envy, but the critical readings — from the Bhārata’s own ambivalence to modern novelists — keep restoring the man the epic refused to flatten.
lore.culturalLegacy: His name is the subcontinent’s standing word for ruinous obstinacy; his friendship with Karṇa, for loyalty across caste. The dice-game is staged as dance-drama across South and Southeast Asia; and in Indonesian wayang, where the Mahābhārata became a national epic, Duryodhana (Duryudana) is among the most beloved characters — the loser the culture refuses to disown.
lore.extendedMeditation: Duryodhana: a name that means “hard to conquer”, worn by the man history conquered most completely. Restored plainly, it keeps its double edge — the boast and the epitaph in four syllables, the epic’s whole tragedy compressed into one who would not yield a needle’s point.
lore.archaeology: Duryodhana’s monuments are performance: the Kutiyattam and Kathakali stages of Kerala keep the dice-game and the embassies in living repertory; and the Indonesian wayang kulit shadow-theatre’s Duryudana puppets are museum-pieces of the epic’s longest journey.
lore.cult: No temples to Duryodhana in orthodox India — the victors’ orthodoxy forbade it. But the epic’s own ambivalence is his cult: he is the character every Mahābhārata retelling must rescue from simplicity.
lore.iconography: The mace-fighter in royal dress, often with Karṇa beside him; in Indonesian wayang, the strong rounded form of the amUK-king. His icon is the clenched fist — the epic’s most repeated gesture of refusal.
lore.reception: Comparative literature sets him beside Achilles and Turnus as the enemy the epic loves; postcolonial readings (Bhyrappa’s Parva, the Indonesian tellings) made his cause the honest one. He remains the great test of the Mahābhārata’s fairness: the reader who hates him has read half the book.
